If you change your mind, you can always re-register your console later using the Xbox Preview Dashboard app.
Here's how to remove your console from the Xbox Preview program:

Open the Xbox Preview Dashboard app. Select Registration. Under Manage flights, select Change.
Note If you have more than one console in the program, you can change their statuses by using Manage other consoles. Under Manage programs, select Remove, and then select Submit. You'll be prompted to select a reason for leaving. If you run into any issues, post in the private Xbox Early Access forums for help.

Note Your console won't be removed from the program until the current Preview update is released to the general public, so it won't happen right away. Until then, your console's status will show as Pending.

I do agree that there is a lot that the game has to offer, but some of the reasoning as to why it's better than the newer iterations of Elder Scrolls I think fall flat.

The narrator talks a bit about the additional depth of gameplay you get from a more complicated, D&D style combat system with some number crunching and random number generation in the background. I would instead argue that what that adds is complexity, and not depth. While there is a more complicated formula being used, does it really add to gameplay? Does it provide meaningful choices to the player? In my opinion, it doesn't.

What I think is more interesting about the modern engine is that it takes out these elements of randomness, which were absolutely necessary in a table-top setting, and puts them directly in the hands of the player. You don't have an X% chance of missing when you swing your sword—whether or not you miss is based on whether you were able to maneuver yourself into an appropriate position when you made your attack. I'm not going to argue that Skyrim does this particularly well, but I think there is something to be said for giving the player more control over the situation, rather than random number generation.

I've always thought that for FPRPGs having a character "hit" an enemy but really miss was silly. I do think that random number generation should be a part of the RPG experience but this abstraction can be better handled by a range of damage or something. Having visual cues not line up at all with what's going on mechanics wise makes no sense.

I completely agree with this sentiment.

There's so often a place for RNG in games, it's hard to imagine a game without any. The point that I was trying to make is that adding the extra RNG on top of a combat system (especially in the hit/miss area) doesn't make it inherently more interesting. It only makes it inherently more complex.

Great video, thanks!

I wouldn't argue that the table-top type game play adds either depth or complexity to the gameplay as its literally the basis of the "game". The game being the formula and rules upon which gameplay is based. In the case of morrowind this is a historical and cultural influence of the time when it was created.

Morrowind is traditionally very deep due to the player being able to manipulate their character and the gameworld around them to solve any problem in just about any way possible. There are not finite or rote solutions to the gameplay decisions given to the player. The complex solutions and even game-breaking solutions using the game's mechanics that even in their absurdity add meaningful and FUN gameplay.
